title: Factors, Common Factors & HCF
summary: One lesson for Set 6 after listing common multiples: list the factors of a number (using the calculator to test each divisor), find common factors from factor pairs, and pick out the HCF. Scaffolding is weaned off through the whiteboards; all questions are authored by hand.

els.text: Test with the calculator. List in order.

A factor of a number divides into it exactly, with no remainder.

Factors come in pairs: $3 \times 8 = 24$, so $3$ and $8$ are both factors of $24$.

$1$ and the number itself are always factors.

slides.title: Testing a factor with the calculator
slides.brief: Type the sum as shown. The fx-85 shows a non-whole answer as a fraction; S⇔D swaps it to a decimal. Build up with each click.

els.text: Testing a factor with the calculator
It shows $6$. A whole number, so $4$ is a factor (and so is $6$).
It shows $\frac{24}{5}$ (or $4.8$ if you press S⇔D). Not whole, so $5$ is not a factor.
Whole number: it is a factor. Fraction or decimal: it is not.

slides.title: Finding all the factors of 24

els.text: Stop when the answer is smaller than the number you divided by.
$4.8$ is smaller than $5$, so stop. Factors of $24$: $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24$

slides.brief: Pupils type 24 ÷ 1, 24 ÷ 2, ... and fill the rows. Stop at 5: the answer is smaller than 5. If the class is quick, check the replay key on the fx-85GT CW to change the divisor without retyping.

question: List all the factors of $48$.
$1\times48,\;2\times24,\;3\times\square$

els.text: A common factor of two numbers is a number that is a factor of both.

slides.title: Find the common factors
slides.brief: Find the factor pairs of each number with the calculator, then circle every number that appears in both. Finish with a calculator check on a number that is not common.

els.text: Write the factor pairs of both numbers. Which numbers are in both?
Calculator check: $18 \div 4 = 4.5$, so $4$ is not a factor of $18$.

slides.title: Discuss

els.text: Kofi says: "The only common factor of $12$ and $18$ is $6$." Is he right?
No. $1$, $2$ and $3$ are common factors too. $1$ is a factor of every number.
Do $8$ and $9$ have a common factor? How do you know?
Yes: $1$. The factors of $8$ are $1, 2, 4, 8$ and of $9$ are $1, 3, 9$. Only $1$ is in both.

slides.brief: Short discussion after the 12 and 18 model. Pupils meet the idea that two numbers can have several common factors, and that 1 is always one of them.

els.text: The highest common factor (HCF) of two numbers is the largest number that is a factor of both.

slides.title: Find the HCF
slides.brief: Reuse the 12 and 18 pairs from the common factors slide: circle the common factors, then pick the highest.

els.text: Find the common factors, then take the highest.
The highest is $6$, so the HCF of $12$ and $18$ is $6$.

slides.title: Discuss

els.text: Ruby says: "The HCF of $12$ and $18$ is $36$." What has she found?
$36$ is in the $12$ and $18$ times tables, so it is a common multiple, not a common factor.
Can the HCF of $12$ and $18$ ever be bigger than $12$? Why not?
No. A factor of $12$ is never bigger than $12$, so the HCF cannot be more than $12$.

slides.brief: Separates the HCF from the common multiples of last lesson: 36 is the first common multiple of 12 and 18.
